items.stem: State what is meant by the term "health-seeking behaviour".
items.answer: The sequence of actions people take to address illness, from self-treatment to consulting healers and doctors
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the sequence of actions people take to address illness, from self-treatment to consulting healers and doctors. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why people in many societies use more than one medical system.
items.answer: Different systems address different aspects of illness (biological symptoms, social causes, spiritual meaning), differ in cost and accessibility, and failure of one prompts resort to another; people combine them pragmatically.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different systems address different aspects of illness (biological symptoms, social causes, spiritual meaning), differ in cost and accessibility, and failure of one prompts resort to another; people combine them pragmatically. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the popular sector and the folk sector.
items.answer: The popular sector is lay care by individuals, families and communities; the folk sector consists of non-professional specialist healers such as herbalists, shamans or bone-setters (Kleinman).
items.markingKey: The popular sector is lay care by individuals, families and communities; the folk sector consists of non-professional specialist healers such as herbalists, shamans or bone-setters (Kleinman). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When baby Amina developed a fever, her grandmother first tied a protective amulet around her wrist and gave her a herbal drink. On the second day, her father bought paracetamol from the kiosk. On the third day, when the fever had not broken, the family borrowed money from an uncle and took her to the district hospital, where she was diagnosed with malaria. "We went to the hospital last because it is far and costly," her mother explained. "But the amulet stays. The medicine kills the fever; the amulet keeps away the eye that sent it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in northern Nigeria.

Using evidence from the text, describe the steps the family takes to treat Amina's fever. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: Day 1: her grandmother ties an amulet and gives a herbal drink; Day 2: her father buys paracetamol from a kiosk; Day 3: the family borrows money from an uncle and takes her to the district hospital, where malaria is diagnosed; the amulet stays on.
items.markingKey: Day 1: her grandmother ties an amulet and gives a herbal drink; Day 2: her father buys paracetamol from a kiosk; Day 3: the family borrows money from an uncle and takes her to the district hospital, where malaria is diagnosed; the amulet stays on. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: A student claims: "People turn to traditional healers only because they cannot afford biomedicine." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Cost matters, but people also choose healers for cultural fit, explanations of "why me", trust and social causes of illness; wealthy people also use multiple systems.
items.markingKey: Cost matters, but people also choose healers for cultural fit, explanations of "why me", trust and social causes of illness; wealthy people also use multiple systems. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Health-seeking behaviour is mainly determined by economic factors."
items.answer: Economic factors set constraints, but cultural explanations and social relations shape choices within them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cost and distance limit choices; structural violence restricts access (Farmer). Arguments against: explanatory models and trust shape choices; kin authority and social relations shape decisions (Janzen). Supported judgement: Economic factors set constraints, but cultural explanations and social relations shape choices within them.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "In Kleinman's model, the lay arena of self-care, family and community where most health decisions are made"?
items.answer: popular sector
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of popular sector.

items.stem: Explain the difference between medical syncretism and medical pluralism.
items.answer: Medical pluralism is the coexistence and combined use of distinct systems; medical syncretism is the blending of elements of systems into a new form, such as healers who combine injections with prayer.
items.markingKey: Medical pluralism is the coexistence and combined use of distinct systems; medical syncretism is the blending of elements of systems into a new form, such as healers who combine injections with prayer. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Lee family in Merced, California shows pluralism and power.
items.answer: Lia's parents used Hmong spiritual healing and herbal remedies alongside, and at times instead of, prescribed anticonvulsants. The hospital's authority and the legal system overrode the family's choices, showing unequal power between systems.
items.markingKey: Context (Lia's parents used Hmong spiritual healing and herbal remedies alongside, and at times instead of, prescribed anticonvulsants.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the hospital's authority and the legal system overrode the family's choices, showing unequal power between systems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to pluralism and power.

Read the text below.

When baby Amina developed a fever, her grandmother first tied a protective amulet around her wrist and gave her a herbal drink. On the second day, her father bought paracetamol from the kiosk. On the third day, when the fever had not broken, the family borrowed money from an uncle and took her to the district hospital, where she was diagnosed with malaria. Explain, with close reference to the text, how the text illustrates medical pluralism and health-seeking behaviour. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: The family follows a hierarchy of resort from home remedies (popular sector) to kiosk medicines to the hospital (professional sector), shaped by cost and distance; decisions involve several kin (grandmother, father, uncle), like a therapy management group; the amulet addresses a different cause (the "eye") so biomedicine and protective practice are combined rather than seen as alternatives.

items.stem: Big question: "Is resistance always possible?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of power and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Farmer's AIDS and Accusation.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: Farmer argues that HIV spread in Haiti along lines of structural violence – poverty, loss of land to the Péligre dam, gender inequality and US economic dominance – not because of "risky culture". It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: Farmer argues that HIV spread in Haiti along lines of structural violence – poverty, loss of land to the Péligre dam, gender inequality and US economic dominance – not because of "risky culture". items.stem: Who first introduced the concept of structural violence (1969)?
items.answer: Johan Galtung
items.markingKey: Johan Galtung. Galtung, a Norwegian peace researcher; Farmer brought it into medical anthropology.

items.stem: Distinguish between structural violence and symbolic violence.
items.answer: Structural violence is harm produced by social and economic structures that deny people's basic needs; symbolic violence is the process by which such inequality is made to seem natural and legitimate, even to its victims.
items.markingKey: Structural violence is harm produced by social and economic structures that deny people's basic needs; symbolic violence is the process by which such inequality is made to seem natural and legitimate, even to its victims. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Health inequality is mainly the result of poor people's unhealthy choices." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Choices are constrained by poverty, work, housing and access to care; structural violence shapes exposure to disease and the options available.
items.markingKey: Choices are constrained by poverty, work, housing and access to care; structural violence shapes exposure to disease and the options available. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The construction workers sleep in a dormitory of bunk beds, twelve to a room, at the edge of the highway. Ravi, who came from Nepal two years ago, shows me the pills he buys from a pharmacy without prescription for his back. "The company doctor only gives a day off if you fall," he says. "Pain is not falling." His friend Bishnu laughs: "Nepalis are strong, we carry mountains." When Bishnu's kidney problem got worse, he was sent home before his contract ended. Ravi sends money to Bishnu's family every month.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a labour camp in a Gulf state.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the text illustrates structural and symbolic violence. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: Structural violence: migrant status, crowded housing, dangerous work and company control over health care produce pain and kidney disease and remove sick workers (Bishnu sent home). Symbolic violence: Bishnu's "Nepalis are strong, we carry mountains" naturalises suffering as an ethnic trait, as Holmes found among Triqui pickers. Ravi's remittances show solidarity under constraint.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Structural violence: migrant status, crowded housing, dangerous work and company control over health care produce pain and kidney disease and remove sick workers (Bishnu sent home). Symbolic violence: Bishnu's "Nepalis are strong, we carry mountains" naturalises suffering as an ethnic trait, as Holmes found among Triqui pickers. Ravi's remittances show solidarity under constraint. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain how Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping illustrates the concept of materiality. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: The hungry body becomes the site where inequality is felt: nervos expresses the weakness, trembling and anger produced by sugar-cane labour and malnutrition.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The hungry body becomes the site where inequality is felt: nervos expresses the weakness, trembling and anger produced by sugar-cane labour and malnutrition. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Nancy Scheper-Hughes, Death without Weeping: The Violence of Everyday Life in Brazil (1992), among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to materiality. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Farmer's account of Acéphie in Do Kay, Haiti as an example, explain structural violence.
items.answer: Acéphie's family lost their land to the Péligre dam; to survive she traded with soldiers, became involved with one, was infected with HIV and died of AIDS. Her death resulted from displacement, poverty, gender inequality and militarisation rather than individual choice.
items.markingKey: Context (Acéphie's family lost their land to the Péligre dam; to survive she traded with soldiers, became involved with one, was infected with HIV and died of AIDS.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: her death resulted from displacement, poverty, gender inequality and militarisation rather than individual choice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structural violence.

items.stem: "Anthropologists studying health inequality have a duty to act, not only to describe." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Engagement is justified and often necessary, provided it is collaborative and transparent.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Farmer combined research with Partners In Health; witnessing suffering carries moral responsibility (Scheper-Hughes); advocacy can compromise analysis; participants should decide what action is wanted. Suitable ethnographies include Farmer's AIDS and Accusation, Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies, Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Engagement is justified and often necessary, provided it is collaborative and transparent. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "Structural violence is the most important cause of ill health in the world." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Structural violence is a major and often neglected cause, but must be combined with other explanations and attention to agency.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: poverty and inequality shape exposure, nutrition and access to care; Farmer, Holmes and Scheper-Hughes document its effects. Arguments against: biological, environmental and genetic factors also matter; the concept can be so broad that it explains everything and nothing; people exercise agency even under structural constraint. Supported judgement: Structural violence is a major and often neglected cause, but must be combined with other explanations and attention to agency. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Briefly explain why symbolic violence helps to sustain health inequality.
items.answer: When those who suffer and those who treat them accept explanations that naturalise suffering (Triqui "bodies made for picking"), inequality is not challenged and the structures producing it continue.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When those who suffer and those who treat them accept explanations that naturalise suffering (Triqui "bodies made for picking"), inequality is not challenged and the structures producing it continue. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why Farmer criticises "cultural" explanations of disease.
items.answer: Blaming the culture of the poor (e.g. "risky" behaviour or belief in sorcery in Haiti) diverts attention from poverty, inequality and international power that actually shape exposure and access to treatment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Blaming the culture of the poor (e.g. "risky" behaviour or belief in sorcery in Haiti) diverts attention from poverty, inequality and international power that actually shape exposure and access to treatment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Compare and contrast the role of power in the text with power in one ethnography you have studied, such as Fassin's When Bodies Remember. Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Migrant workers may lose their jobs or visas if identified as critical; the company and country should be anonymised; health information is confidential; the researcher must avoid exposing workers to employer retaliation. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "safe and dignified burial"?
options: Involving local people and leaders in designing and running health interventions so that they are trusted and appropriate
The WHO-promoted approach during the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic that adapted funeral practices to prevent transmission while respecting religious and family obligations
Bourdieu's term for domination that is accepted as natural by those dominated, as when inequalities are explained by the supposed characteristics of the victims
Johan Galtung's term (1969), developed by Paul Farmer, for harm done to people by social structures – poverty, racism, gender inequality – that prevent them from meeting their basic needs
items.answer: The WHO-promoted approach during the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic that adapted funeral practices to prevent transmission while respecting religious and family obligations
items.markingKey: B. "safe and dignified burial" is the WHO-promoted approach during the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic that adapted funeral practices to prevent transmission while respecting religious and family obligations.

items.stem: Explain why epidemics often produce blame and stigma.
items.answer: Fear seeks a cause, and blame is directed at marginalised groups or other nations (Haitians and AIDS), reflecting existing power relations and classifications.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fear seeks a cause, and blame is directed at marginalised groups or other nations (Haitians and AIDS), reflecting existing power relations and classifications. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Global health programmes are culturally neutral." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They carry assumptions about bodies, risk and behaviour, and their categories and priorities reflect the power of donors and international organisations.
items.markingKey: They carry assumptions about bodies, risk and behaviour, and their categories and priorities reflect the power of donors and international organisations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When the health team arrived in white suits to take Pa Sesay's body, his sons blocked the path. "He will not go in a plastic bag like rubbish," the eldest said. After hours of talk, the team leader agreed that the imam could pray over the body and that the family could watch the burial from behind a rope. The sons dug the grave themselves. Weeks later, the village set up its own checkpoint, and Mamie Kamara, the women's leader, insisted that anyone returning from the city stay in a hut by the stream for twenty-one days.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2015 Ebola epidemic.

Describe, with examples from the text, how the burial of Pa Sesay was negotiated. Organise your answer as a series of clearly separated descriptive points.
items.answer: The sons blocked the health team in white suits; they objected to the body going "in a plastic bag like rubbish"; after hours of talk the team allowed the imam to pray and the family to watch from behind a rope; the sons dug the grave; later the village set up a checkpoint and a 21-day stay for returnees.

Analyse how the text illustrates change in response to an epidemic. Support your answer with evidence from the text. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Initial resistance reflected the obligation to bury the dead with dignity; negotiation produced a compromise similar to "safe and dignified burial", combining biomedical rules with religious rites; the village then made its own quarantine rules (21 days, the incubation period), showing local adaptation and leadership (Mamie Kamara) – Richards's "people's science".

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Local knowledge is as important as biomedical knowledge in controlling epidemics."
items.answer: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: communities adapted burial practices to stop Ebola (Richards); trust determines whether interventions are accepted. Arguments against: biomedical knowledge identified pathogens, vaccines and treatments; local knowledge can include harmful practices or rumours. Supported judgement: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Involving local people and leaders in designing and running health interventions so that they are trusted and appropriate"?
items.answer: community engagement
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of community engagement.

items.stem: Distinguish between a top-down health intervention and a community-led health intervention.
items.answer: A top-down intervention is designed and imposed by outside authorities, often efficiently but with little local trust; a community-led intervention is shaped by local people, building trust and fit, though it may be slower to scale.
items.markingKey: A top-down intervention is designed and imposed by outside authorities, often efficiently but with little local trust; a community-led intervention is shaped by local people, building trust and fit, though it may be slower to scale. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Richards's study of Ebola in Sierra Leone, explain how it illustrates local responses to epidemics.
items.answer: Villagers developed their own quarantine, caregiving and burial adaptations, and cases fell where communities and responders co-operated. A "people's science" of observation and adaptation complemented biomedical knowledge and helped end the epidemic.
items.markingKey: Context (Villagers developed their own quarantine, caregiving and burial adaptations, and cases fell where communities and responders co-operated.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a "people's science" of observation and adaptation complemented biomedical knowledge and helped end the epidemic. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to local responses to epidemics.

items.stem: Identify one way in which change matters in Fassin's When Bodies Remember (in South Africa during the AIDS epidemic and the controversy over President Thabo Mbeki's AIDS policies (around 2000)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Activism by the Treatment Action Campaign (founded 1998) and court rulings forced the state to provide antiretroviral drugs, changing the politics of health.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Activism by the Treatment Action Campaign (founded 1998) and court rulings forced the state to provide antiretroviral drugs, changing the politics of health. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Paul Farmer co-founded which health organisation in 1987?
items.answer: Partners In Health
items.markingKey: A. Partners In Health began in Haiti.

items.stem: Distinguish between direct violence and structural violence.
items.answer: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted by identifiable actors; structural violence is harm caused indirectly by social arrangements, with no single perpetrator.
items.markingKey: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted by identifiable actors; structural violence is harm caused indirectly by social arrangements, with no single perpetrator. items.stem: Briefly explain why health-seeking decisions are often collective.
items.answer: Illness affects families economically and socially; kin share costs, transport and knowledge, and senior relatives may hold authority over decisions (Janzen's therapy management group).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Illness affects families economically and socially; kin share costs, transport and knowledge, and senior relatives may hold authority over decisions (Janzen's therapy management group). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a community-led health intervention and a top-down health intervention.
items.answer: A top-down intervention is designed and imposed by outside authorities, often efficiently but with little local trust; a community-led intervention is shaped by local people, building trust and fit, though it may be slower to scale.
items.markingKey: A top-down intervention is designed and imposed by outside authorities, often efficiently but with little local trust; a community-led intervention is shaped by local people, building trust and fit, though it may be slower to scale. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Priya writes: "Structural violence means the same thing as poverty." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Structural violence includes poverty but also racism, gender inequality, political repression and legal status, and emphasises that these are socially produced harms.
items.markingKey: Structural violence includes poverty but also racism, gender inequality, political repression and legal status, and emphasises that these are socially produced harms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why medical pluralism involves power relations.
items.answer: Systems are not equal: biomedicine usually has state backing, while others may be marginalised or banned; doctors may dismiss other healers, and patients may hide their use of them.

items.stem: Explain why top-down epidemic responses can fail.
items.answer: They may ignore local knowledge, violate cultural obligations (e.g. burial rites), rely on coercion that breeds distrust, and overlook the structural conditions – poverty, weak health systems – that drive the epidemic.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The construction workers sleep in a dormitory of bunk beds, twelve to a room, at the edge of the highway. Ravi, who came from Nepal two years ago, shows me the pills he buys from a pharmacy without prescription for his back. "The company doctor only gives a day off if you fall," he says. "Pain is not falling." His friend Bishnu laughs: "Nepalis are strong, we carry mountains." When Bishnu's kidney problem got worse, he was sent home before his contract ended. Ravi sends money to Bishnu's family every month.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a labour camp in a Gulf state.

Explain how the text illustrates structural and symbolic violence, using one or more anthropological concepts. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Structural violence: migrant status, crowded housing, dangerous work and company control over health care produce pain and kidney disease and remove sick workers (Bishnu sent home). Symbolic violence: Bishnu's "Nepalis are strong, we carry mountains" naturalises suffering as an ethnic trait, as Holmes found among Triqui pickers. Ravi's remittances show solidarity under constraint.

items.stem:

When the health team arrived in white suits to take Pa Sesay's body, his sons blocked the path. "He will not go in a plastic bag like rubbish," the eldest said. After hours of talk, the team leader agreed that the imam could pray over the body and that the family could watch the burial from behind a rope. The sons dug the grave themselves. Weeks later, the village set up its own checkpoint, and Mamie Kamara, the women's leader, insisted that anyone returning from the city stay in a hut by the stream for twenty-one days.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2015 Ebola epidemic.

Using the key concept of change, explain how the text illustrates change in response to an epidemic. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Initial resistance reflected the obligation to bury the dead with dignity; negotiation produced a compromise similar to "safe and dignified burial", combining biomedical rules with religious rites; the village then made its own quarantine rules (21 days, the incubation period), showing local adaptation and leadership (Mamie Kamara) – Richards's "people's science".

items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Didier Fassin, When Bodies Remember: Experiences and Politics of AIDS in South Africa (2007) and Paul Farmer, AIDS and Accusation: Haiti and the Geography of Blame (1992).
items.answer: Fassin's When Bodies Remember (in South Africa during the AIDS epidemic and the controversy over President Thabo Mbeki's AIDS policies (around 2000)): Fassin links the epidemic to the "embodied history" of apartheid – migrant labour, poverty and violence – and analyses why AIDS denialism found support as a response to racist representations. items.stem: Compare and contrast how classification is shown in Arthur Kleinman, Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture (1980) and Paul Farmer, AIDS and Accusation: Haiti and the Geography of Blame (1992).

items.stem: Explain why structural violence is described as "invisible".
items.answer: It is built into ordinary institutions and economic arrangements, has no single identifiable perpetrator, and its effects (illness, early death) appear as natural or as individual misfortune, so its causes are hidden.

When baby Amina developed a fever, her grandmother first tied a protective amulet around her wrist and gave her a herbal drink. On the second day, her father bought paracetamol from the kiosk. On the third day, when the fever had not broken, the family borrowed money from an uncle and took her to the district hospital, where she was diagnosed with malaria. "We went to the hospital last because it is far and costly," her mother explained. "But the amulet stays. The medicine kills the fever; the amulet keeps away the eye that sent it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in northern Nigeria.

Analyse how the text illustrates medical pluralism and health-seeking behaviour. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.

Ethnography – John Janzen, The Quest for Therapy in Lower Zaire (1978), among BaKongo communities of Lower Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), fieldwork 1960s: Decisions about treatment were taken not by the patient alone but by a "therapy management group" of kin who negotiated which healers to consult. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that local knowledge is as important as biomedical knowledge in controlling epidemics. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: communities adapted burial practices to stop Ebola (Richards); trust determines whether interventions are accepted; biomedical knowledge identified pathogens, vaccines and treatments; local knowledge can include harmful practices or rumours. Suitable ethnographies include Richards's Ebola, Farmer's AIDS and Accusation, Lindenbaum's Kuru Sorcery. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "Is resistance always possible?" With reference to Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping and the key concept of power, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: She describes the "everyday violence" of poverty, in which hunger is medicalised as nervos and treated with tranquillisers and vitamins, hiding the political causes of suffering. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When baby Amina developed a fever, her grandmother first tied a protective amulet around her wrist and gave her a herbal drink. On the second day, her father bought paracetamol from the kiosk. On the third day, when the fever had not broken, the family borrowed money from an uncle and took her to the district hospital, where she was diagnosed with malaria. "We went to the hospital last because it is far and costly," her mother explained. "But the amulet stays. The medicine kills the fever; the amulet keeps away the eye that sent it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in northern Nigeria.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.
items.answer: The child is a minor and the account involves health and household finances; consent from parents, anonymity, and care not to portray the delay as ignorance (which could stigmatise the family) are needed. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
